# Rearranging formulas {#sec-rearranging}

::: {.goals}
Goals

- Rearrange a formula so that a different variable stands alone.
- Use the same steps as for equations with numbers, keeping letters as letters.
- Recognise when a formula has to be rearranged with a power or a root.
:::

::: {.video minutes="9"}
Rearranging formulas
:::

## One formula, many questions

A formula connects several quantities. The markup formula from Session 1 connects the price $p$, the cost $c$ and the markup rate $m$:

$$p = c\,(1 + m)$$

Written like this, it answers "what is the price?". But a business may also ask "what is the highest cost I can accept?" or "which markup am I actually charging?". Each question needs the formula solved for a different letter. **Rearranging** (or *transposing*) a formula uses exactly the same balancing steps as solving an equation; you just keep the other letters as they are.

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: three versions of the markup formula
Start from $p = c\,(1 + m)$.

**Solve for $c$** (divide both sides by $1 + m$):
$$c = \frac{p}{1 + m}$$
A shop that wants to sell a bike for €364 with a markup of 40 % can pay at most $\frac{364}{1.40} = 260$ euros for it.

**Solve for $m$:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
p &= c\,(1 + m) &&\mid :c\\
\frac{p}{c} &= 1 + m &&\mid -1\\
m &= \frac{p}{c} - 1
\end{aligned}
$$
A tune-up that costs €28 and sells for €42 has a markup of $\frac{42}{28} - 1 = 0.5 = 50\,\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## A trick when you get lost
If you are unsure about a step, try it with numbers first. Does $p = c\,(1 + m)$ really become $c = \frac{p}{1 + m}$? Take $c = 100$, $m = 0.2$: then $p = 120$, and $\frac{120}{1.2} = 100$. ✓
:::

## Formulas with brackets and several terms

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: break-even for any business
Profit is $P = (p - v)\,q - F$. Solve for $q$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= (p - v)\,q - F &&\mid +F\\
P + F &= (p - v)\,q &&\mid :(p - v)\\
q &= \frac{P + F}{p - v}
\end{aligned}
$$

For $P = 0$ this is the break-even formula $\frac{F}{p - v}$ from @sec-linear. Note the condition: we may only divide by $p - v$ if it is not zero. If the price equals the variable cost, there is no contribution margin, and no volume will ever cover the fixed costs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake: "cancelling" across a plus sign
From $q = \frac{P + F}{p - v}$ you **cannot** cancel to get $\frac{P}{p} + \frac{F}{-v}$ or anything similar. A fraction can only be split along the numerator: $\frac{P + F}{p - v} = \frac{P}{p - v} + \frac{F}{p - v}$. The denominator stays whole.
:::

## Formulas with powers

Some formulas contain the unknown in a power. You undo a power with a root, and you already know the tool from Session 1.

::: {.callout-note}
## Worked example: compound growth, solved three ways
An amount $K_0$ that grows by the rate $i$ per year for $n$ years becomes

$$K_n = K_0\,(1 + i)^n$$

This formula is the heart of Session 4. It can be rearranged in three useful ways:

| Question | Solve for | Result |
|------------------------------------------|:-----:|-------------------------------------|
| How much will it be worth?              | $K_n$ | $K_n = K_0\,(1 + i)^n$ (as given) |
| How much must I invest today?           | $K_0$ | $K_0 = \dfrac{K_n}{(1 + i)^n}$ |
| Which yearly rate gets me there?        | $i$   | $i = \left(\dfrac{K_n}{K_0}\right)^{1/n} - 1$ |

The last line is the average growth rate from @sec-powers. The second line has a name you will meet again: the **present value**. Solving for $n$ ("how many years?") needs logarithms, which come in Session 3.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check yourself

1. Solve $\text{gross} = \text{net} \cdot (1 + t)$ for the VAT rate $t$.

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   Divide by net: $\frac{\text{gross}}{\text{net}} = 1 + t$, so $t = \frac{\text{gross}}{\text{net}} - 1$.
   :::

2. Revenue is $R = p \cdot q$. Solve for $p$ and explain what it means.

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $p = \frac{R}{q}$: the price is revenue per unit, for example the average price you received.
   :::

3. Solve the cost formula $C = F + v\,q$ for $v$.

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $C - F = v\,q$, so $v = \frac{C - F}{q}$ (for $q \neq 0$).
   :::

4. How much must you invest today at 4 % a year to have €10,000 in 3 years?

   ::: {.hidden-solution}
   $K_0 = \frac{10\,000}{1.04^3} = \frac{10\,000}{1.124864} \approx 8\,889.96$, so about **€8,889.96**.
   :::
:::
